items.title: 53342_Cozy Cole oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I guess around the same time that you guys were doing that in New York, Lee Young was going through a similar thing in Hollywood.

ctx.x: Well yes, and then they were trying to get that thing going there, John Hammond, so you didn't think too much about it, you know, because it wasn't any sort of prejudice or anything else evident up there when you were playing, because they all treated you beautiful. See Raymond, and then all the guys in the band, you know, just everybody up there just treated you wonderful, so you didn't feel that pressure at all.
I guess around the same time that you guys were doing that in New York, Lee Young was going through a similar thing in Hollywood.
Yeah, but that was afterward, though, wasn't it? Wasn't that after?

items.title: 53279_Lee Young Oral History Interview
items.q: I used to meet Cozy every morning at 11 o'clock with my practice pad and my drum guide, and we would go through -- we'd go through the book together.

ctx.x: Were black patrons allowed to come to the Famous Door?

Now you see, that I don't really know, because I could, you know, being a musician, because I would go to work with Cozy Cole almost every night, and any drummer that could hold the stick I went to hear him play, you know, because I felt as though that I could learn as much from the bad drummers as I did from the good drummers. I learned things not to do, you know, not to become sloppy and not to get lazy and you know, have pride in your playing. But I learned so much from Cozy, because Cozy -- he was a practice…

See, Cozy was a rudimental drummer, you know, and so he was a stickler for rudiments. And I think that basically, he really did help me because I'm not sure if I would have been as good as reading if I had not spent hours and hours with Cozy, because that's all we would do - just stay in the book, stay in the book.
